cards.front: What are sealed classes for, and since when?
cards.back: They restrict who may extend them via permits; preview in Java 15, standard in Java 17
cards.extra: A sealed hierarchy is a closed set of subtypes, which lets the compiler check exhaustiveness in switch and prevents third-party subclassing.

cards.front: What is a record, and when did it become standard?
cards.back: A concise immutable data class — components become private final fields with a canonical constructor and accessors; standard since Java 16
cards.extra: Records also generate equals, hashCode and toString. They are shallowly immutable: a mutable component still needs care.

cards.front: What does pattern matching for instanceof remove?
cards.back: The redundant cast — if (o instanceof String s) declares s already typed
cards.extra: Standard in Java 16. The variable's scope is limited to where the type test is known to have succeeded.

cards.front: What is a text block?
cards.back: A multi-line string literal delimited by triple quotes, with incidental indentation removed — final in Java 15
cards.extra: It removes the escaping and concatenation of long SQL or JSON literals while preserving indentation relative to the closing delimiter.

cards.front: What did switch expressions change about switch?
cards.back: A switch can now produce a value, use arrow labels without fall-through, and yield from a block — final in Java 14
cards.extra: Arrow labels removed the most common switch bug: a missing break falling into the next case.

cards.front: What are hidden classes (Java 15)?
cards.back: Classes that cannot be referenced by other classes' bytecode — created at run time for frameworks that generate code
cards.extra: Lambdas are implemented this way. They are not discoverable by name and can be unloaded independently, which helps frameworks that churn classes.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::05 Other JVM Tools

cards.front: What is a multi-release JAR?
cards.back: A JAR holding several versions of the same class, selected at run time by the JVM version — Java 9
cards.extra: The manifest attribute Multi-Release: true plus a versioned directory structure lets one artifact serve several Java versions.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::05 Other JVM Tools

cards.front: What happened to the Nashorn JavaScript engine?
cards.back: Deprecated in Java 11 and removed in Java 15
cards.extra: It had been added in Java 8 to replace Rhino. GraalVM's JavaScript support is the successor for embedding.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::05 Other JVM Tools

cards.front: What is the helpful NullPointerException?
cards.back: JVM messages that name the exact expression that was null — Java 14, on by default since 15
cards.extra: Instead of a bare line number you get "because 'user.address' is null", which usually identifies the bug immediately.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: What improvements did Java 9 make to the Process API?
cards.back: ProcessHandle: pid, parent, children, command line, start time, and onExit() as a CompletableFuture
cards.extra: Before this, querying or waiting on a process was awkward and platform-dependent.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Why allow private methods in interfaces (Java 9)?
cards.back: So several default methods can share code without exposing the helper as part of the API
cards.extra: Before, a shared helper had to be public or duplicated. Private interface methods are not inherited.

cards.front: What is a marker interface?
cards.back: An interface with no methods, used to tag a class — Serializable, Cloneable
cards.extra: It gives the type system something to test with instanceof, and it can be combined with annotations.

cards.front: Does final on an array freeze its elements?
cards.back: No — it freezes the reference; the elements remain assignable
cards.extra: final int[] a = {1,2}; a[0] = 9; compiles. Only a = new int[]{} is rejected.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.front: When does an instance initializer block run relative to the constructor?
cards.back: Before the constructor body, after super(), in source order for multiple blocks
cards.extra: It is the place for initialisation shared by every constructor — but it cannot see constructor parameters.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::19 Initializer Block

cards.front: What is the main thread?
cards.back: The thread the JVM creates to run main(); it is a user (non-daemon) thread
cards.extra: It is the last user thread to finish in a normal program — when it ends and no other user threads remain, the JVM exits.

cards.front: What does Thread.join() do?
cards.back: Blocks the calling thread until the target thread terminates
cards.extra: Overloads take a timeout. It is the standard way to wait for a worker before reading its result.

cards.front: What is the difference between interrupt and stop?
cards.back: interrupt() is cooperative — it sets a flag or throws InterruptedException; stop() was removed as unsafe
cards.extra: Code must check the flag or handle the exception. An interrupt does not by itself kill a running thread.

cards.front: What does ThreadGroup do?
cards.back: Groups threads into a tree so operations and limits can be applied to a set
cards.extra: It is largely obsolete: uncaughtException handling and ExecutorService replaced its useful parts.

cards.front: What does Optional express?
cards.back: That a value may be absent, forcing the caller to handle that case explicitly
cards.extra: Use it for return types, not fields or parameters. orElseThrow and map replace null checks readably.

cards.front: How does a method reference differ from a lambda?
cards.back: It is shorthand for a lambda that only calls an existing method: System.out::println
cards.extra: Four forms: static, bound instance, unbound instance (String::length), and constructor (ArrayList::new).
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: What is HttpURLConnection?
cards.back: An abstract class for HTTP-specific URL connections: methods, headers, response codes, streaming bodies
cards.extra: It is the pre-Java-11 API; java.net.http.HttpClient is the modern replacement.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::03 Networking in Java

cards.front: What is JMH, and what problem does it solve?
cards.back: The Java Microbenchmark Harness — it warms up, forks JVMs and prevents dead-code elimination
cards.extra: Timing code by hand measures the JIT more than the code: early runs are slow, later ones may be optimised away entirely.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: What does the module system add over packages?
cards.back: Explicit dependencies and exports: a module states what it requires and what it makes visible — Java 9
cards.extra: Packages have no dependency declaration, and public members are visible to everyone. Modules add strong encapsulation on top.
